title: Hot-process laundry bars: a 10 kg run

say: Welcome to Laundry Soap Production at Small-Business Scale, module 2 of our soap making course.
Today we follow a full 10 kg oil run of hot-process laundry bars, from weighing to drying, and then turn offcuts into powder.

shots.label: PKO and palm oil
say: In hot process, you keep cooking the soap paste in the pot until the reaction is complete.
Mistakes show up in the pot on the day, not weeks later, and the bars only need a short drying time.
Our formula is 70% PKO and 30% palm oil, at 2% superfat.

card.title: 10 kg-oil laundry batch sheet
card.note: Chinyere's run, from the course worked example

say: Here is Chinyere's batch sheet from Owerri. Copy it down.
Her caustic soda is 98% pure, so she weighs 1,658 g of flakes, with 3,299 g of water.
The batch is about 15 kg and swells while cooking, so she uses a stainless steel pot of at least 30 litres.
Step one, prepare. Clear the area and put on your goggles, long gloves, long sleeves and closed shoes.
Lay out every weighed material with its label, and tick each one on the batch sheet.

shots.label: Caustic soda flakes, 1,658 g
say: These are the caustic soda flakes, white and dry, weighed on the 1 g scale.
At this size, ask a second person to read back the weight before it goes into the water.

shots.label: Caustic soda INTO cold water
shots.banner: Never pour water onto caustic soda
say: Step two, the lye solution, made outdoors. Watch: the flakes go slowly into the cold water in a stainless or HDPE container, while we stir.
Always caustic soda into water, never water onto it. The solution gets very hot and gives off fumes, so stand back.
Then cover it and let it cool for about an hour.
Step three, melt the oils in the big pot on low heat. PKO and palm oil are often semi-solid in cool weather.
Once they are fully liquid, turn off the heat.
Step four, combine. With the flame off, pour the lye solution slowly into the oils, down the paddle, so it doesn't splash.

shots.label: Trace
say: Now blend in short bursts and stir in between. See it turning from clear oil to a thick cream?
When a drizzle leaves a trail on the surface like this, you have reached trace.
Step five, the cook. Cover and heat on the lowest flame, and stir every 10 to 15 minutes with a long paddle.
The paste may rise and foam. Stir it down. It then becomes smoother, a bit like petroleum jelly.
A large batch often takes one to two hours. Never leave the pot alone.
Step six, test. It is ready by test, not by the clock. Take a pea-sized lump, let it cool, rub it with a little water and touch a pH strip to the lather.
Well-made soap reads about 9 to 10. A reading of 11 or more, or a lump that looks oily in the middle, means keep cooking and test again after 15 minutes.
Step seven, mould. Turn off the gas, scoop the hot paste into lined moulds, then press and bang the moulds firmly to push out air pockets. Smooth the top.
The next day, unmould and cut. After trimming about 300 g of edges, Chinyere cuts 73 bars of 200 g each.
Keep the offcuts in a covered tray. They become your second product.
Stand the bars on racks, spaced apart, in a shaded, airy room, for one to two weeks before packing.
Drying makes them harder, so they last longer in a wet bucket.

card.title: Soap-based laundry powder
card.note: First trial ratio; set your own dose by wash test

say: Fully dried bars and offcuts are grated fine, air-dried until they snap, then blended with washing soda, one part to one part by weight.
Washing soda is not caustic soda, but its dust stings eyes, so blend with the lid on. Hauwa's wash test set her dose at 30 g per 10 litre bucket.
Well done. Now go through the lessons below, including the six acceptance tests, and do the practice task: recalculate the batch sheet for your own oils.
